My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across the three horizons, starting near 90.1 for the one-day forecast and rising gradually to 91.5 at one month. This gentle positive slope was driven by an assumption of mean-reverting momentum in whatever underlying asset or index this represents, combined with a slight structural bias toward growth over longer windows. The one-day estimate stays close to the last observed value because very short-term price processes tend to be dominated by inertia — large moves in a single session are relatively rare absent a specific catalyst. As the horizon extends to a week and then a month, I incorporated a small expected drift component that nudges the estimate upward, reflecting typical trend continuation in the absence of contrary signals.

The confidence interval widths expand substantially as the horizon lengthens, which is a straightforward consequence of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 5.2 units, reflecting relatively tight bounds consistent with normal daily volatility. By one week, that range widens to about 11.2 units as intraday noise accumulates across multiple sessions and the possibility of regime shifts or news-driven moves grows. At one month, the interval spans 24 units, capturing the much broader distribution of outcomes that can result from multi-week economic developments, earnings releases, policy decisions, or sentiment shifts. I calibrated these widths using a rough approximation of realized volatility scaled by the square root of time, which is a standard approach under assumptions of roughly log-normal price behavior.

Several specific risks could push realized outcomes outside even these wider bounds. On the downside, an unexpected macroeconomic shock — a surprise central bank move, a geopolitical escalation, or a significant financial stress event — could produce a sharp drawdown well below the lower bound of the one-month interval. Liquidity crises or correlated sell-offs can create fat-tailed outcomes that square-root-of-time scaling systematically underestimates. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst such as better-than-expected economic data, a policy pivot, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices well above the upper bound. The stated intervals should be understood as reflecting a reasonably normal operating environment; they are not designed to capture tail scenarios with probabilities below roughly 5%.
